group.title: Academic precision
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: Although.
wrong: He agreed, albeit happily and with no doubts at all.

words.meaning: Made or done for one purpose, not planned in advance.
wrong: The ad hoc plan was carefully prepared years in advance.

words.meaning: Existing in fact, though not officially.
examples: English is the {de facto} language of business.
wrong: He is the de facto leader because he was officially elected.

words.meaning: Real and genuine.
wrong: It’s a bona fide offer, so it’s fake.

words.meaning: By itself; in itself.
wrong: Money isn’t bad per se, which means money is always bad.

words.meaning: Most noticeable or important.
wrong: These are the salient points, so they are minor.

words.meaning: Only slightly connected to the main subject.
examples: His remarks were {tangential} to the debate.
wrong: The comment was tangential, so it was central to the topic.

words.meaning: Depending on something else.
wrong: The deal is contingent on approval, so it will happen no matter what.

words.meaning: In proportion to something.
wrong: His pay is commensurate with his experience: very high pay for no experience.

words.meaning: Happening together with something else.
wrong: Growth brought concomitant risks that appeared years before it.

words.meaning: A result that follows naturally from something else.
examples: A {corollary} of lower taxes is less public money.
wrong: A corollary is a cause that has no result.

words.meaning: Very different and not connected.
wrong: The two ideas are disparate, so they are almost identical.

words.meaning: Regularly found in a place or group.
wrong: The disease is endemic, so it never appears there.

words.meaning: To estimate something unknown from known facts.
examples: We can {extrapolate} future trends from this data.
wrong: We extrapolated the trend without looking at any data.

words.meaning: A simple rule that helps you decide or learn.
examples: A useful {heuristic} is to check the source first.
wrong: A heuristic is a long, exact formula that solves every case.

words.meaning: Looking at the whole rather than separate parts.
wrong: A holistic approach looks at only one small part.

words.meaning: Belonging to the basic nature of something.
wrong: The ring has intrinsic value only because my grandmother wore it.

words.meaning: Present but not yet active or visible.
wrong: His talent is latent, so everyone has already seen it.

words.meaning: Countless; very many.
examples: There are {myriad} ways to solve it.
wrong: There are myriad ways: exactly two.

words.meaning: Relating to rules about how things should be.
wrong: The essay makes a normative claim by only describing what is.

words.meaning: Following accepted beliefs.
wrong: Her methods are orthodox, so they break every tradition.

words.meaning: To prevent something from happening.
wrong: The rule precludes it, so it is fully allowed.

words.meaning: Based on something.
wrong: The plan is predicated on growth, which has no part in it.

words.meaning: Able to be measured.
wrong: The results are quantifiable, so nobody can measure them.

words.meaning: Making something complex seem too simple.
wrong: It’s a reductive view, so it shows all the complexity.

words.meaning: Needed for a purpose.
wrong: She has the requisite skills, so she can’t do the job.

words.meaning: To include something in a larger group.
wrong: The small team was subsumed into finance, so it stayed fully separate.

words.meaning: Combined effect greater than the parts.
examples: The merger created {synergy} between the teams.
wrong: Synergy means the parts work worse together.

words.meaning: Equal in effect to something worse.
wrong: Silence is tantamount to agreement, so silence means you disagree.

words.meaning: A principle or belief.
examples: Honesty is a key {tenet} of journalism.
wrong: A tenet is a random opinion with no importance.

words.meaning: Never having happened before.
wrong: It was unprecedented, so it had happened many times before.

words.meaning: The appearance of being true or real.
examples: The details add {verisimilitude} to the novel.
wrong: The silly details give the novel verisimilitude, so it feels completely fake.

words.meaning: A statement accepted as true without proof.
examples: It’s an {axiom} that hard work pays.
wrong: An axiom is a claim that must be proven before anyone accepts it.

words.meaning: To understand words or actions in a particular way.
wrong: His silence was construed as consent, though nobody gave it any meaning.

words.meaning: To notice or understand something not obvious.
examples: I could {discern} a note of anger.
wrong: I could discern the shouting easily; it was the loudest thing in the room.

words.meaning: To get information or a reaction from someone.
wrong: The question elicited a reply by getting no response at all.

words.meaning: To explain in detail.
examples: The essay {explicates} the poem line by line.
wrong: The essay explicates the poem by saying nothing about it.

words.meaning: To suggest something as a basis for argument.
examples: The theory {posits} that time is relative.
wrong: The theory posits nothing, so it suggests that time is relative.

words.meaning: To claim to be something, often falsely.
examples: The letter {purports} to be from the bank.
wrong: The letter purports to be from the bank, which it truly is.

words.meaning: Therefore.
examples: He was absent; {ergo}, he missed the test.
wrong: He was present; ergo, he missed the test.

words.meaning: Mentioned earlier.
wrong: The aforementioned report will be mentioned for the first time next week.

words.meaning: A complete change in the usual way of thinking.
examples: The internet caused a {paradigm shift} in retail.
wrong: A paradigm shift is a tiny change that nobody notices.

words.meaning: Instead of.
examples: Staff got extra leave {in lieu of} pay.
wrong: Staff got extra leave in lieu of extra leave.

words.meaning: Aware of something.
wrong: We are cognizant of the risks, so we have no idea they exist.

words.meaning: The state of being everywhere.
examples: The {ubiquity} of phones has changed manners.
wrong: The ubiquity of phones means they are very hard to find.
